edges.effect_quant: Telephone coaching improved several targeted behavior outcomes in randomized trials, including 86.8 more minutes per week of moderate leisure activity in low-active older adults and modest improvements in BMI, waist circumference, physical activity, vegetable intake, and self-management in post-coronary patients; a cardiac-rehabilitation adjunct also produced greater medium-term weight loss in higher-risk participants (1.6 kg vs 0.4 kg in those with BMI at least 25 kg/m2).
edges.population: adults receiving telephone-delivered coaching for physical activity, weight management, self-management, or other health behaviors
edges.mechanism: Telephone coaching lowers the access barrier for repeated behavior-change support. Short counseling calls can provide accountability, troubleshooting, and goal revision without clinic visits, which helps some people sustain physical activity or diet changes that would otherwise drift.
edges.summary: The best overall reading is that telephone health coaching works, but usually modestly. Trials across older adults, cardiac populations, and rehabilitation referrals show that repeated phone contact can improve activity, weight-related outcomes, and selected self-management behaviors, especially when it is structured and repeated rather than purely informational.
edges.caveats: Telephone coaching is not a magic format on its own: intensity, population, and comparator matter a lot. Benefits are often behavior-specific and moderate in size, so this edge should be read as a practical delivery strategy for lifestyle support rather than a guarantee of broad clinical transformation.
